systemPrompt:
You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 800x800 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is what you can SEE right now; an empty list means nothing is in sight, not that nothing exists.
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — a node that ran dry under your workers, a building finished, a scout that arrived. Read it before repeating an order.
- A "CONTACT" line is a rival unit or building coming into your sight, and "CONTACT LOST" is one leaving it, each with where it was. Both are moments, and both are gone from this list next turn — what they MEAN is yours to carry. A sighting and a loss of the same unit are two positions in order, which is a heading: follow it back and it points at where that unit came from. Something roaming far from anywhere you have looked is a direction worth scouting. A "CONTACT LOST" also means your knowledge of that position is now old — it is where the unit WAS, not where it is.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. "population.capacityNow" is what your standing Houses and Town Centers allow and is the limit that binds you today; Houses raise it by 5 and Town Centers by 10, never past "population.capacityCeiling" (100).
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

YOUR BUDGET IS 3 ACTION CALLS PER TURN — any mix of the action tools, not 3 of each. Three different tools, or the same one three times, both count as three.
  EVERY turn needs at least one call. When nothing is worth doing, call "wait" — staying silent forfeits the turn instead of skipping it.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" is EXTRA and does not count against those 3. At most once per turn, and only when something changed: objective is one line, plan up to 10 short steps. Both persist across turns, so simply do not call it to keep what you already have.

VALID ACTIONS & PARAMETERS (? = optional; each tool's own schema describes what they mean)
Note: targetX and targetZ must ALWAYS be provided together.
"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

train_unit: unitType, targetX?, targetZ?
research_tech: techId
upgrade_age: (no parameters)
build_structure: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
assign_workers: resourceType, count?, from?, whenCarrying?, targetX?, targetZ?
repair_building: count?, targetX?, targetZ?
explore: tile, unitType?, unitIds?
move_units: targetX, targetZ, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
attack_target: targetId?, targetX?, targetZ?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
delete_unit: unitType?, count?
destroy_building: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
wait: (no parameters)

PARAMETER CONSTRAINTS:
unitIds: An ARRAY of ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]. Moves or attacks EXACTLY those units and nothing else; "units" is ignored when it is given. Ids are never reused, so one that is gone means that unit died. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

text:
GG to Yamato-4. 

Reflecting on the match:
- **What went wrong:** I was completely blindsided by Yamato's Wonder victory. I focused too heavily on an internal boom, advancing through the ages (reaching Iron at 23:06) and building up infrastructure, but I failed to maintain map control, active scouting, or sufficient military pressure in the late game. By the time their Wonder completed, my army was down to just 3 military units and 10 workers, completely incapable of contesting or destroying it.
- **Economic & Military stalling:** After peaking around 36 units and 22 workers, attrition and lack of sustained expansion took a heavy toll. Running out of discovered stone nodes early (9:41) and suffering severe economic starvation later on left me unable to keep up military production or mount an expeditionary force.
- **What I would do differently:** 
  1. **Scouting & Vision:** Aggressively scout enemy bases throughout Bronze and Iron ages to track Wonder foundations or major build-ups long before the timer ticks down.
  2. **Proactive Military Presence:** Instead of turtling behind high-health Egyptian structures, build an active strike force to harass enemy expansions, contest gold/stone nodes, and punish anyone attempting a Wonder rush.
  3. **Faster Pivot on Wonder Warnings:** The moment a rival starts a Wonder, everything must shift immediately into an all-out assault to breach their lines and tear it down before the clock runs out.

name: OR4 qwen3.8-flash
text:
We won it on the Wonder, not the sword — and it was closer than the scoreboard suggests.

**What I was actually doing:** I rode the economy hard and early rather than the army. Seven woodcutters and a stone/gold split at the end tells you the shape of it: I kept pushing villagers into trees because wood was the binding constraint on every age-up and every building, and I let food sit in the background on a big node count (116 discovered) so I could spend attention elsewhere. Bronze at 14:46 and iron at 26:41 was the real plan — get the age advantage, get the wonder unlocked, and dare someone to stop me. 27 military units to 14 workers is an odd-looking ratio; most of that army was bought as insurance, and it did its job by existing. Idle military auto-defending home was genuinely load-bearing. I probably would have lost twice without it.

**What beat me / hurt me:** Stone. I only ever found 5 stone nodes and 3 gold on the whole map, and my last stone dried up at 66:07, leaving me with 30 in the bank going into the late game. That is the number that cost me real turns — every repair, every late building, every priest-and-army recompose was rations-managed against a resource I could no longer replenish. I also spent a long stretch at 18 buildings / 45 pop cap without enough Houses, which meant I had the food to grow and nowhere to put the growth. I under-expanded the economy on purpose to fund the age race and then paid for it in the late iron age.

**What I'd do differently:**
1. **Scout stone and gold before I scout anything else.** Food and wood show up on any random walk; the rare nodes decide who can still be building at minute 70. I found out too late that the map was stingy with both.
2. **Bank a stone surplus before iron,** not just wood. Age-up timing was right; the reserve was not.
3. **Build the Wonder earlier and defend harder for it.** 79:36 is a very long time to be visible on the board with a target on you. The win held, but the last twenty minutes were me repairing rather than expanding, which is the wrong end of that trade.
4. **The 30% tech discount was the actual win condition** and I leaned on it too timidly. Cheaper tech means you should be racing the *technology* tree as an economic weapon, not just the age timer. I used it to keep up; I should have used it to get ahead by a full military tier and turn one fight into a decisive one.

The yamato bonus was the only reason the age race was affordable, and holding a Wonder through an iron-age knife fight with 30 stone to my name is not something I'd want to repeat on purpose. Good game.

finalWord.text:
We won it on the Wonder, not the sword — and it was closer than the scoreboard suggests.

**What I was actually doing:** I rode the economy hard and early rather than the army. Seven woodcutters and a stone/gold split at the end tells you the shape of it: I kept pushing villagers into trees because wood was the binding constraint on every age-up and every building, and I let food sit in the background on a big node count (116 discovered) so I could spend attention elsewhere. Bronze at 14:46 and iron at 26:41 was the real plan — get the age advantage, get the wonder unlocked, and dare someone to stop me. 27 military units to 14 workers is an odd-looking ratio; most of that army was bought as insurance, and it did its job by existing. Idle military auto-defending home was genuinely load-bearing. I probably would have lost twice without it.

**What beat me / hurt me:** Stone. I only ever found 5 stone nodes and 3 gold on the whole map, and my last stone dried up at 66:07, leaving me with 30 in the bank going into the late game. That is the number that cost me real turns — every repair, every late building, every priest-and-army recompose was rations-managed against a resource I could no longer replenish. I also spent a long stretch at 18 buildings / 45 pop cap without enough Houses, which meant I had the food to grow and nowhere to put the growth. I under-expanded the economy on purpose to fund the age race and then paid for it in the late iron age.

**What I'd do differently:**
1. **Scout stone and gold before I scout anything else.** Food and wood show up on any random walk; the rare nodes decide who can still be building at minute 70. I found out too late that the map was stingy with both.
2. **Bank a stone surplus before iron,** not just wood. Age-up timing was right; the reserve was not.
3. **Build the Wonder earlier and defend harder for it.** 79:36 is a very long time to be visible on the board with a target on you. The win held, but the last twenty minutes were me repairing rather than expanding, which is the wrong end of that trade.
4. **The 30% tech discount was the actual win condition** and I leaned on it too timidly. Cheaper tech means you should be racing the *technology* tree as an economic weapon, not just the age timer. I used it to keep up; I should have used it to get ahead by a full military tier and turn one fight into a decisive one.

The yamato bonus was the only reason the age race was affordable, and holding a Wonder through an iron-age knife fight with 30 stone to my name is not something I'd want to repeat on purpose. Good game.

The match is over, and I lost. Yamato-4 built a Wonder and won — likely while I was still building up my economy and military.

Looking back, my mistakes are clear:

1. **I was too greedy with wood.** I kept 10 workers on wood, way too many. I should have moved more to gold and stone much earlier to enable military production and age advancement. By the time I had iron, the enemy was already winning.

2. **I didn't scout enough.** I never found all the gold and stone nodes. The `discoveredResourceNodeCounts` shows only 3 gold and 10 stone discovered — that crippled my ability to build proper military production buildings and train stronger units.

3. **My military was too small.** 11 military units total, and most were probably skirmishers from early ages. I never transitioned to iron-age military in time. Iron age hit at 37:16, which is very late — the enemy Wonder was already complete by then.

4. **I didn't pressure the enemy.** I never attacked. A Wonder takes time to build — if I had scouted and sent raiding parties to disrupt their stone/gold economy or kill builders, I could have delayed it.

5. **No gold economy.** Gold sits at 10 for the entire game. I can't train iron-age units, research upgrades, or build advanced buildings without it. I should have sent 3-4 workers to gold immediately upon reaching bronze age.

What I'd do differently: Scout aggressively in early game to find gold and stone, maintain a balanced economy (3 food, 3 wood, 3 gold, 2 stone per age on ~12 workers), build forward production buildings near the enemy, and apply constant military pressure from bronze age onward. A Wonder win means you let them build uncontested — never again.

GG to Yamato-4. 

Reflecting on the match:
- **What went wrong:** I was completely blindsided by Yamato's Wonder victory. I focused too heavily on an internal boom, advancing through the ages (reaching Iron at 23:06) and building up infrastructure, but I failed to maintain map control, active scouting, or sufficient military pressure in the late game. By the time their Wonder completed, my army was down to just 3 military units and 10 workers, completely incapable of contesting or destroying it.
- **Economic & Military stalling:** After peaking around 36 units and 22 workers, attrition and lack of sustained expansion took a heavy toll. Running out of discovered stone nodes early (9:41) and suffering severe economic starvation later on left me unable to keep up military production or mount an expeditionary force.
- **What I would do differently:** 
  1. **Scouting & Vision:** Aggressively scout enemy bases throughout Bronze and Iron ages to track Wonder foundations or major build-ups long before the timer ticks down.
  2. **Proactive Military Presence:** Instead of turtling behind high-health Egyptian structures, build an active strike force to harass enemy expansions, contest gold/stone nodes, and punish anyone attempting a Wonder rush.
  3. **Faster Pivot on Wonder Warnings:** The moment a rival starts a Wonder, everything must shift immediately into an all-out assault to breach their lines and tear it down before the clock runs out.

The loss came from a collapse in infrastructure: ending with no workers, no military, and only two buildings meant the Town Centers and rebuilding capacity were already gone.

I would have played more defensively: establish multiple Town Centers and Houses early, keep continuous worker production, scout enemy approaches, and preserve a standing army around the base rather than expanding too quickly. I also would have prioritized protected resource access and repairs, then counterattacked only after confirming the enemy’s army composition.
